name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,174

clue.text: Male sheep turned to face English horse

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: a ram is a male sheep
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A ram swings round to square up to an English horse in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: The turned sheep is placed so that it faces, that is stands in front of, the English letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A mare is an adult female horse, so the general word is a plain hypernym for it.

clue.text: Control way something is done with speed

blocks.note: a mode is a manner or method of doing something
rate means pace or speed

explanation.surface: Advice to keep a grip on how fast a job gets done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Control' reads as a noun heading the phrase, but it is a verb standing alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To moderate something is to restrain or keep it within limits, which is a verb sense of control.

clue.text: Big defeat — manager finally dismissed

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word, so only its closing letter is kept

blocks.note: the closing letter of manager
a batsman who is dismissed in cricket is out

explanation.surface: After a heavy loss the team's manager is sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the sacking a consequence of the defeat; in fact 'dismissed' is the cricket term for being out.
explanation.definitionFit: A rout is a decisive, overwhelming loss in which the losing side is put to flight.

clue.text: Apple and fish for celebrity to tuck into

indicators.note: whatever tucks into something goes inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: the cod is a common food fish
a star is a celebrity

explanation.surface: A menu of apple and fish laid on for a famous guest to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the celebrity a diner, but the celebrity is the piece that goes inside the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Costard is an old English variety of large cooking apple, so the answer is an example of the fruit.

clue.text: Smart class getting rid of idiot always

indicators.note: to get rid of something is to throw it out, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: taken as written
an ass is a fool
ever means always, as in 'for ever'

explanation.surface: A bright class that is always shedding its dimmest member.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the fool out of the class leaves just CL, which then joins EVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Smart in the sense of intelligent or quick-witted is a common synonym for the answer.

clue.text: Eight new lads misbehaving pretend to be ill

indicators.note: misbehaving means acting out of order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A group of eight unruly new boys fake sickness to dodge school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' looks like a description of the lads, but its letters belong in the mix along with 'Eight' and 'lads'.
explanation.definitionFit: Swing the lead is a British idiom meaning to shirk work, typically by feigning sickness or injury.

clue.text: Welcome signal, nothing obscure

blocks.note: first meaning: the signal that danger has passed
second meaning: everything plain to see, with no part hidden

explanation.walkthrough: Read the second phrase literally: if nothing is obscure then every part is plain.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the siren sounded after an air raid and also describes a state where everything is understood.

clue.text: Blue feathers

blocks.note: first meaning: sad or depressed
second meaning: the soft fine plumage of birds

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue feathers' looks like a description of a bird's colouring; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means low in spirits and also names the fluffy under-plumage used to fill pillows.

clue.text: Provision for someone to sit in Derbyshire town

blocks.note: first meaning: a deep padded sofa with arms and back of equal height
second meaning: a market town in the English county of Derbyshire, famous for its crooked spire

explanation.surface: Arranging seating for a visitor in a Midlands town.
explanation.walkthrough: Derbyshire is a county in the English Midlands; the sofa style takes its name from an Earl of Chesterfield.
explanation.definitionFit: A chesterfield is a type of buttoned leather sofa, which is furniture provided for people to sit on.

clue.text: Female who’s joined someone’s son at a match

definitions.text: Female who’s joined someone’s son at a match

blocks.clueFragment: Female who’s joined someone’s son at a match
blocks.note: surface reading: a woman partnering a friend's boy at a sports fixture or game
setter's reading: a match is a marriage, so she has wed the son and become part of his parents' family

explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' suggests sport, but here it is a marriage; the woman is defined by her relation to the son's parents.
explanation.definitionFit: A son's wife becomes a legal relative of his parents, which is exactly what this family term names.

clue.text: Observe some of those experts

indicators.note: only some of the following letters are needed, a run lying inside the words

blocks.note: the end of 'those' and the start of 'experts'

explanation.surface: An invitation to watch a group of specialists at work.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe something is to look at or notice it, a direct synonym of the answer.

clue.text: A man is one acting on behalf of others

definitions.text: one acting on behalf of others

blocks.note: taken as written
GENT is short for gentleman, a polite word for a man

explanation.surface: A statement that a certain man represents other people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A man' reads as one phrase, but the article and the noun each give their own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent is a representative who negotiates or does business for clients, such as a literary or sports agent.

clue.text: What is made by grannies working?

indicators.note: working suggests being worked over or kneaded, so these letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about what elderly women knit or bake while busy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What is made' suggests handicrafts, but 'made' is in the sense of money made; 'working' also reads as having a job.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnings are the money a person makes, as in making a living from wages or profit.

clue.text: Once again deal with unwanted military manoeuvre

blocks.note: the prefix re- means again
to treat a matter is to deal with it

explanation.surface: Having to tackle a dreaded army exercise one more time.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half of the clue also reads as a pun: to retreat is literally to treat again.
explanation.definitionFit: A retreat is a withdrawal of troops from the enemy, a movement no commander wants to make.

clue.text: Period in America, end point of travel

blocks.note: a term is a period of time
taken as written
US is the abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: A spell spent in the States, the final stop on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a connecting word, but it supplies its own letters to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminus is the last station on a rail or bus route, where the journey stops.

clue.text: Listener’s part involved a murder

indicators.note: involved means tangled or intricate, so these letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An eavesdropper's role was implicated in a killing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listener's part' sounds like a role in a crime story, but it is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The eardrum is the membrane in the ear that vibrates with sound, so it is an anatomical part of anyone hearing.

clue.text: Fellow hiding holy books in cloak

indicators.note: to hide something you cover it up, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: a fellow is a male person
NT is the New Testament, a collection of holy books

explanation.surface: A man concealing scriptures under his cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' could be MAN, which also starts the answer, but the letters only fit when the fellow is MALE split around the books.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantle is a loose sleeveless cloak, so the two words are near synonyms.

clue.text: Panic with leader deposed? That’s wrong

definitions.note: a noun here, as in 'a wrong'

indicators.note: a deposed leader is removed from the front, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: terror is extreme fear or panic

explanation.surface: Fear spreads after a ruler is overthrown, and someone protests it was unjust.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as political commentary; 'leader' just means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An error is a mistake, and a wrong in the sense of an incorrect act is a close synonym.

clue.text: Tool everyone picked up

indicators.note: to pick something up can mean to hear it, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: everyone means all people

explanation.surface: A tool that every person grabbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' looks like physically lifting the tool, but it means hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: An awl is a small pointed hand implement for piercing holes in leather or wood.

clue.text: Back of his vehicle shows evidence of damage

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of 'his'
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: The rear of a man's car has been dented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back of his vehicle' reads as one phrase about a car's rear, but 'Back of' applies only to 'his'.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is a mark left after a wound heals, so it is a sign that harm was once done.

clue.text: Company not likely to collapse

blocks.note: first meaning: a business
second meaning: solid and stable

explanation.surface: A business that looks financially secure.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a company's finances; the second sense is physical solidity.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a business partnership and also describes something steady, solid and unyielding.

clue.text: Opposing money allowance — student studying hard needs it

blocks.note: con means against, as in 'pros and cons'
a cent is a unit of money
a ration is a fixed allowance

explanation.surface: Arguing against a pocket-money allowance, since a hard-working student needs one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' looks like it refers back to the allowance, but the whole final phrase is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard study demands focused mental attention, so the definition describes the answer by its use.

clue.text: What is left in lodge outside university

indicators.note: being outside means surrounding, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: to lodge somewhere is to reside there
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Something left behind in a porter's lodge just off campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lodge' reads as a noun, a gatehouse, but it is the verb meaning to live somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A residue is the small amount that remains after the main part has gone or been used up.

clue.text: Birds contributing to the music

indicators.note: something contributing to a whole forms part of it, so the letters lie inside the words

blocks.note: the end of 'the' and the start of 'music'

explanation.surface: Birdsong forming part of the music.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests songbirds, but these are large flightless birds that do not sing.
explanation.definitionFit: Emus are large flightless Australian birds, so they are an example of the general class.
